caption:
The top scorer on South Korea's national tax accountant exam says he cheated with a miniature camera, a generative AI tool and a smartphone.
He got 159 of 160 first round questions right. Police are now investigating and the government wants to suspend his certificate.

Should exams ban every smart device in the room?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

paragraphs.text: The top scorer on South Korea's 63rd national tax accountant qualification exam admitted on November 15, 2026 that he cheated using electronic devices and generative AI, according to Korea JoongAng Daily and The Korea Herald. The confession came in a video released on the YouTube channel of his attorney, Lee Don-ho of Nova Law Firm.
The Korea Herald reported that the man is 34. In the video he apologized for the harm he had caused and said his top ranking was not the result of honest effort, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.

In the first stage of the exam, held in April, he scored 397.5 out of 400 and answered 159 of 160 multiple-choice questions correctly, both outlets reported. His only miss was in public finance. He earned perfect marks in introductory tax law, a section where the 16,856 examinees averaged 30.18 points and about 74 percent fell below the 40-point minimum. He also placed first in the essay-based second stage in July, with 663 out of 800.

Doubts grew after he posted his results on his blog and shared his preparation with local media on November 11. Fellow candidates and practicing tax accountants questioned the scores, and critics online pointed to study materials that showed little wear, according to The Korea Herald. He first denied cheating and said he had solved unfamiliar questions by elimination. On November 13, the Human Resources Development Service of Korea, which runs the exam, said a review of his first-stage grading had found no irregularities.
How he says he did it

According to his account, he photographed exam questions with a miniature camera, sent the images to a generative AI system and checked the answers on his smartphone. He said he used the method in both stages of the tax exam and in the first stage of the certified public accountant exam in March, which he did not pass. He sat near the front of the exam room, and proctors were present. He declined to give further technical details, saying others might copy the method.
He told viewers he had faced financial strain after leaving a job to start a business and felt anxious about how long it would take to pass, Korea JoongAng Daily reported.

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency received his written confession through his attorney and assigned the case to its Provincial Special Detective Corps on November 15. He said he would hand over his remaining devices as evidence; some had been damaged. The Ministry of Economy and Finance plans to suspend his certificate through a review committee under the National Tax Service, saying a confession alone is not enough for a formal revocation. Under the Certified Tax Accountant Act, cheating candidates have their results voided and are barred from the exam for five years.

The presidential office said it was taking the matter seriously and was considering measures for other tests, including the national college entrance exam scheduled for November 19. The Korea Herald reported that five other people were caught using unauthorized equipment on state certification tests this year.

The case shows how little hardware it now takes to turn a paper exam into an open-book test. A small camera and a phone were enough to pass two proctored rounds and an official grading review. Exams that rely on metal detectors and room supervision were not built for answers that arrive from a chatbot in seconds.
The next test is South Korea's college entrance exam on November 19, where the government is weighing new checks for AI devices.
